title: Definition of done, and what "it works on my machine" costs the team

videos.script: Ana finishes the allergens ticket. She opens the menu page in her browser, and there it is: a little picture showing which items contain gluten, milk and eggs. It works. She pushes, and moves the card to review. {{works}} An hour later, Bruno opens the same branch, and the picture is not there. {{broken}} It works on my machine is probably the most famous sentence in software, and it is almost always true. It did work on Ana's machine. The problem is that nobody else has Ana's machine. {{famous}} This lesson is about the gap between it works for me and it is done, and who pays for that gap when nobody names it. Usually it is not the person who said done. {{gap}} You will see one of the most common ways it happens in Git: a file that was never committed. And you will see a simple way to catch it: clone your own branch somewhere fresh, and look. {{catch}} Then you will see how teams make that check automatic, with a machine that belongs to nobody and runs on every pull request. {{ci}} And you will see the agreement that ties it all together, the definition of done. It is one list, written once, that says what done means on this team, so nobody has to guess. {{title}}
